<script>
  // Restore the saved color scheme preference, or
  // enact the browser preference if "automatic", 
  // without expecting DOM load to have completed.
  //
  // Also restore any saved readingmode and ToC display preferences.
  function initializeReadingPreferences() {
    let saved_theme = localStorage.getItem("ar5iv_theme") || "automatic";
    if (saved_theme === "automatic") {
      if (window.matchMedia("(prefers-color-scheme: dark)").matches) {
        saved_theme = "dark";
      }
    }
    if (saved_theme == "dark") {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "dark");
    } else {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "light");
    }

    const tocDisplay = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_toc_display');
    if (tocDisplay) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-toc-display", tocDisplay);
    }
    const readingMode = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_reading_mode');
    if (readingMode) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-reading-mode", readingMode);
    }
    // Pre-apply spinout-banner dismissal here, before the banner paints, so it
    // never flashes in only to be hidden later by the deferred arxiv-header.js.
    // Key matches arxiv-header.js: "arxiv-banner-dismissed:" + data-banner-name.
    if (localStorage.getItem('arxiv-banner-dismissed:spinout-nonprofit')) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-banner-dismissed", "");
    }
  }
  // Run as soon as JS starts, to minimize repainting
  initializeReadingPreferences();
</script>

<article class="ltx_document ltx_authors_1line">
<h1 class="ltx_title ltx_title_document">Non-Interfering Weight Fields: Treating Model Parameters as a Continuously Extensible Function</h1>
<div class="ltx_authors">
<span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Sarim Chaudhry
</span><span class="ltx_author_notes"><span class="ltx_author_notes_content">
<span class="ltx_contact ltx_role_affiliation"><span class="ltx_contact_name">Affiliation: </span>Purdue University
</span>
<span class="ltx_contact ltx_role_email"><span class="ltx_contact_name">Email: </span><a href="mailto:"><span id="id1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">chaud158@purdue.edu</span></a>
</span></span></span></span></div>

<div id="abstract1" class="ltx_abstract"><h6 class="ltx_title ltx_title_abstract">Abstract</h6>
    
<p id="abstract1.1" class="ltx_p">Large language models store all learned knowledge in a single, fixed weight vector. Teaching a model new capabilities requires modifying those same weights, inevitably degrading previously acquired knowledge. This fundamental limitation, known as catastrophic forgetting, has resisted principled solutions for decades. Existing approaches treat weights as immutable artifacts that must be protected through techniques like regularization heuristics, replay buffers, or isolated adapter modules. The problem is none of these provide a structural guarantee against forgetting. In this work, we propose Non-Interfering Weight Fields (NIWF), a framework that replaces the fixed weight paradigm with a learned function that generates weight configurations on demand from a continuous capability coordinate space. After training on a task, we commit the occupied coordinate region by snapshotting the field’s outputs on anchor points to enforce a functional lock during all future training. We validate NIWF on sequential instruction-following and code generation tasks using Mistral-7B, demonstrating zero forgetting on committed tasks with competitive perplexity on new tasks. The framework introduces the notion of software-like versioning for neural network intelligence, where capabilities can be committed, extended, composed, and rolled back without retraining.</p>
  
</div>
<section id="S1" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">1 </span>Introduction</h2>

<figure id="S1.F1" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2602.18628v1/Non_Interfering_Weight_Fields.svg" id="S1.F1.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/342;" width="476" height="342"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 1: </span>The NIWF architecture. A frozen backbone processes tokens
through a two-pass forward. The coordinate dynamics module produces
a capability coordinate <math id="S1.F1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="z" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>z</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">z</annotation></semantics></math> from mean-pooled hidden states. The
weight field maps <math id="S1.F1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="z" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>z</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">z</annotation></semantics></math> to sparse gating over low-rank adapter bases.
After training, coordinate regions are committed and functionally
locked via anchor-based snapshot constraints.</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Consider the current workflow for improving a deployed language model. A team identifies a deficiency in the model’s mathematical reasoning. They collect training data, fine-tune the model, and evaluate. The math performance will improve, but now it has subtly become worse at creative writing, code generation, and a dozen other capabilities. This is the default behavior of gradient-based learning on neural networks, and it has been documented extensively since the earliest connectionist systems <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">McCloskey and Cohen, 1989</a>; <a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ratcliff, 1990</a>; <a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">French, 1999</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">A neural network encodes everything it knows in a single weight vector <math id="S1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W\in\mathbb{R}^{d}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>W</mi><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mi>d</mi></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W\in\mathbb{R}^{d}</annotation></semantics></math>. Every gradient update to teach a new capability modifies the same numbers that encode existing capabilities. There is no separation between the substrate and the content. This results in every write being potentially destructive.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">The field has developed numerous techniques to mitigate this problem. Elastic Weight Consolidation (EWC) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kirkpatrick et al., 2017</a>)</cite> penalizes changes to weights deemed important for prior tasks, but these importance estimates can be noisy and the penalty is often too soft. Progressive Neural Networks <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">Rusu et al., 2016</a>)</cite> freeze old columns and add new ones, but parameter cost grows linearly with the number of tasks. Experience replay <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Rolnick et al., 2019</a>; <a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chaudhry et al., 2019</a>)</cite> maintains a buffer of old data, but provides no formal guarantee against forgetting. Low-rank adapters (LoRA) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hu et al., 2022</a>)</cite> and their variants <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">Dettmers et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhang et al., 2023</a>)</cite> offer parameter-efficient fine-tuning but are static patches with no routing, no versioning, and no continual learning story. Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architectures <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">Shazeer et al., 2017</a>; <a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">Fedus et al., 2022</a>; <a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">Dai et al., 2024</a>)</cite> route tokens to discrete experts but have no concept of committing regions or preventing interference across training stages.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">None of these approaches address the fundamental issue. They all treat the weight vector as the primary object and try to protect it through external mechanisms. We propose a different starting point entirely.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p5.1" class="ltx_p">In this paper, we introduce Non-Interfering Weight Fields (NIWF), a framework that replaces the fixed weight paradigm with a learned, continuously extensible function over a capability coordinate space. The core insight is simple but consequential. Instead of storing knowledge as weights, we store it as a function that generates weights. Different inputs navigate to different coordinates in this space, and different coordinates produce different weight configurations. New learning extends the function into unoccupied territory rather than overwriting existing mappings. Old regions are functionally frozen, making catastrophic forgetting structurally impossible rather than merely unlikely.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p6.1" class="ltx_p">Our contributions are as follows.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p7" class="ltx_para">
<ul id="S1.I1" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="S1.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We formalize the concept of a weight field, a learned mapping <math id="S1.I1.i1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="F_{\theta}:\mathbb{R}^{d_{z}}\to\mathbb{R}^{L\times N_{b}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>F</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mrow><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>z</mi></msub></msup><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mrow><mi>L</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msub><mi>N</mi><mi>b</mi></msub></mrow></msup></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">F_{\theta}:\mathbb{R}^{d_{z}}\to\mathbb{R}^{L\times N_{b}}</annotation></semantics></math> that generates sparse gating decisions over banks of low-rank adapter bases conditioned on a capability coordinate <math id="S1.I1.i1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="z" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>z</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">z</annotation></semantics></math>. We show that this formulation cleanly separates stored capacity (total bases) from active computation (top-<math id="S1.I1.i1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> selection), enabling monotonic capacity growth without proportional compute increase.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We introduce a region commitment protocol that provides a hard, non-approximate guarantee against catastrophic forgetting. After training on a task, the occupied region of coordinate space is snapshotted and functionally locked. During all future training, the field must reproduce the exact same outputs for coordinates within the locked region. This is enforced through a mean-squared-error loss on anchor points.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We design a recurrent coordinate dynamics module that navigates the capability space conditioned on the model’s hidden states, enabling input-dependent weight generation without external task labels or routing signals.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i4" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We implement and validate the complete framework on Mistral-7B <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">Jiang et al., 2023</a>)</cite>, demonstrating the complete process of train, commit, extend, and evaluate on sequential instruction-following and code generation tasks with zero degradation on committed capabilities.</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">2 </span>Related Work</h2>

<section id="S2.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.1 </span>Catastrophic Forgetting and Continual Learning</h3>

<div id="S2.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The problem of catastrophic forgetting was identified in early connectionist research <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">McCloskey and Cohen, 1989</a>; <a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ratcliff, 1990</a>)</cite> and has remained central to neural network research ever since. <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">French (1999)</a></cite> provides a comprehensive survey of early approaches. Modern continual learning methods broadly fall into three categories.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Regularization-based methods add terms to the loss function that penalize changes to parameters important for prior tasks. EWC <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kirkpatrick et al., 2017</a>)</cite> uses the diagonal of the Fisher information matrix as an importance measure. Synaptic Intelligence (SI) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zenke et al., 2017</a>)</cite> accumulates per-parameter importance online during training. Memory Aware Synapses (MAS) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">Aljundi et al., 2018</a>)</cite> estimates importance based on sensitivity of learned function outputs. These methods provide soft protection that degrades as the number of tasks grows, since the regularization terms from different tasks eventually conflict.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Replay-based methods maintain a buffer of examples from prior tasks and interleave them during training on new tasks. Experience replay <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Rolnick et al., 2019</a>)</cite>, A-GEM <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chaudhry et al., 2019</a>)</cite>, and DER++ <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">Buzzega et al., 2020</a>)</cite> represent this family. While effective in practice, replay does not provide guarantees and requires storing potentially sensitive data from prior tasks.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Architecture-based methods allocate dedicated capacity for each task. Progressive Neural Networks <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">Rusu et al., 2016</a>)</cite> add new columns for each task with lateral connections. PackNet <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">Mallya and Lazebnik, 2018</a>)</cite> prunes and freezes subnetworks. These methods provide stronger guarantees but scale poorly. NIWF is closest in spirit to architecture-based methods but achieves the separation through a continuous functional mapping rather than discrete module allocation, avoiding the linear parameter growth problem.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.2 </span>Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning</h3>

<div id="S2.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">LoRA <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hu et al., 2022</a>)</cite> introduced the idea of freezing pretrained weights and training low-rank additive updates. Subsequent work has explored quantized variants <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">Dettmers et al., 2023</a>)</cite>, adaptive rank allocation <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhang et al., 2023</a>)</cite>, and composition of multiple adapters <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">Huang et al., 2023</a>)</cite>. However, all LoRA variants produce a single static delta that is applied identically regardless of input. There is no mechanism for input-dependent routing, no notion of region locking, and no built-in continual learning capability. NIWF can be viewed as a conditional, routed, and versionable generalization of LoRA, where the static delta is replaced by a dynamically generated mixture over a bank of low-rank bases.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.3 </span>Mixture-of-Experts</h3>

<div id="S2.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Sparse MoE models <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">Shazeer et al., 2017</a>; <a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lepikhin et al., 2021</a>; <a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">Fedus et al., 2022</a>; <a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">Dai et al., 2024</a>)</cite> route tokens to specialized expert subnetworks via a learned gating function. Recent work has explored gating mechanisms in attention specifically, including Switch Heads <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">Csordas et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, Native Sparse Attention <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib28" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yuan et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, and gated attention variants <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib29" title="" class="ltx_ref">Qiu et al., 2025</a>)</cite>. These architectures demonstrate the value of conditional computation but operate at the token level within a single training stage. They have no concept of committing routing decisions across training stages, and expert parameters remain mutable throughout training.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS4" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.4 </span>Hypernetworks</h3>

<div id="S2.SS4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Hypernetworks <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ha et al., 2017</a>)</cite> generate weights for a target network using a secondary network. HyperTransformers <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ivison and Peters, 2022</a>)</cite> and related work <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">von Oswald et al., 2020</a>)</cite> have explored hypernetworks for few-shot learning and task-conditional generation. NIWF extends this line of work by (a) generating sparse gating decisions over low-rank bases rather than full weight matrices, making the approach practical for large language models, (b) introducing a continuous coordinate space with recurrent dynamics, and (c) adding region commitment and functional locking as first-class operations.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S3" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">3 </span>Method</h2>

<div id="S3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We now describe the NIWF framework in detail. The system consists of four components, a frozen pretrained backbone <math id="S3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{B}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℬ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{B}</annotation></semantics></math>, a bank of low-rank adapter bases <math id="S3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\{A_{b},B_{b}\}_{b=1}^{N_{b}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msub><mi>A</mi><mi>b</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>B</mi><mi>b</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><msub><mi>N</mi><mi>b</mi></msub></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\{A_{b},B_{b}\}_{b=1}^{N_{b}}</annotation></semantics></math> per target module, a weight field <math id="S3.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="F_{\theta}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>F</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">F_{\theta}</annotation></semantics></math> that maps capability coordinates to gating decisions, and a coordinate dynamics module <math id="S3.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="G_{\phi}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>G</mi><mi>ϕ</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">G_{\phi}</annotation></semantics></math> that navigates the coordinate space conditioned on the model’s internal representations.</p>
</div>
<section id="S3.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.1 </span>Frozen Backbone with Conditional Adapter Banks</h3>

<div id="S3.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Let <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{B}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℬ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{B}</annotation></semantics></math> denote a pretrained language model with all parameters frozen. We identify a set of target linear modules within <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{B}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℬ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{B}</annotation></semantics></math>, typically the query, key, value, output, gate, up, and down projections in each transformer layer. For a target module with weight matrix <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W_{\text{base}}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{out}}\times d_{\text{in}}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>W</mi><mtext>base</mtext></msub><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mrow><msub><mi>d</mi><mtext>out</mtext></msub><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msub><mi>d</mi><mtext>in</mtext></msub></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W_{\text{base}}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{out}}\times d_{\text{in}}}</annotation></semantics></math>, we introduce a bank of <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N_{b}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>N</mi><mi>b</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N_{b}</annotation></semantics></math> low-rank adapter bases, each parameterized by a pair of factor matrices:</p>
<table id="S3.E1" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E1.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="A_{b}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{out}}\times r},\quad B_{b}\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times d_{\text{in}}},\quad b=1,\ldots,N_{b}" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>A</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mi>b</mi></msub><mo>∈</mo><mi>ℝ</mi><msup><mrow></mrow><mrow><msub><mi>d</mi><mtext>out</mtext></msub><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>r</mi></mrow></msup><mo rspace="1.167em">,</mo><mi>B</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mi>b</mi></msub><mo>∈</mo><mi>ℝ</mi><msup><mrow></mrow><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msub><mi>d</mi><mtext>in</mtext></msub></mrow></msup><mo rspace="1.167em">,</mo><mi>b</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>N</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mi>b</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">A_{b}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{out}}\times r},\quad B_{b}\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times d_{\text{in}}},\quad b=1,\ldots,N_{b}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(1)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS1.p1.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r\ll\min(d_{\text{in}},d_{\text{out}})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo>≪</mo><mrow><mi>min</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>d</mi><mtext>in</mtext></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>d</mi><mtext>out</mtext></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r\ll\min(d_{\text{in}},d_{\text{out}})</annotation></semantics></math> is the rank. Each pair defines a low-rank weight delta <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Delta W_{b}=A_{b}B_{b}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{out}}\times d_{\text{in}}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>W</mi><mi>b</mi></msub></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>A</mi><mi>b</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>B</mi><mi>b</mi></msub></mrow><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mrow><msub><mi>d</mi><mtext>out</mtext></msub><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msub><mi>d</mi><mtext>in</mtext></msub></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Delta W_{b}=A_{b}B_{b}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{out}}\times d_{\text{in}}}</annotation></semantics></math>. Following <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hu et al. (2022)</a></cite>, we initialize <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="B_{b}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>B</mi><mi>b</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">B_{b}</annotation></semantics></math> with Kaiming uniform and <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="A_{b}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>A</mi><mi>b</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">A_{b}</annotation></semantics></math> with zeros, ensuring that the initial delta is zero and training starts from the pretrained model’s behavior.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Given a gating vector that selects the top-<math id="S3.SS1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> bases with indices <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{S}\subset\{1,\ldots,N_{b}\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒮</mi><mo>⊂</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>N</mi><mi>b</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{S}\subset\{1,\ldots,N_{b}\}</annotation></semantics></math> and associated weights <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\{w_{b}\}_{b\in\mathcal{S}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msub><mi>w</mi><mi>b</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒮</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\{w_{b}\}_{b\in\mathcal{S}}</annotation></semantics></math> (normalized via softmax over the selected logits), the effective output of the adapted module on input <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x\in\mathbb{R}^{B\times T\times d_{\text{in}}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mrow><mi>B</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>T</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msub><mi>d</mi><mtext>in</mtext></msub></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x\in\mathbb{R}^{B\times T\times d_{\text{in}}}</annotation></semantics></math> is:</p>
<table id="S3.E2" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="y=W_{\text{base}}x+\frac{\alpha}{r}\sum_{b\in\mathcal{S}}w_{b}\cdot xB_{b}^{\top}A_{b}^{\top}" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>W</mi><mtext>base</mtext></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mrow><mrow><mfrac><mi>α</mi><mi>r</mi></mfrac><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><munder><mo movablelimits="false">∑</mo><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒮</mi></mrow></munder><msub><mi>w</mi><mi>b</mi></msub></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">⋅</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msubsup><mi>B</mi><mi>b</mi><mo>⊤</mo></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msubsup><mi>A</mi><mi>b</mi><mo>⊤</mo></msubsup></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y=W_{\text{base}}x+\frac{\alpha}{r}\sum_{b\in\mathcal{S}}w_{b}\cdot xB_{b}^{\top}A_{b}^{\top}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(2)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS1.p2.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>α</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\alpha</annotation></semantics></math> is a scaling hyperparameter analogous to the LoRA scaling factor.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">A key implementation detail concerns memory efficiency. A naive implementation would gather the selected adapter matrices as tensors of shape <math id="S3.SS1.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="[B,T,k,d_{\text{out}},r]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mi>B</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>T</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>k</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>d</mi><mtext>out</mtext></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>r</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">[B,T,k,d_{\text{out}},r]</annotation></semantics></math>, which for MLP projections with <math id="S3.SS1.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="d_{\text{out}}=14336" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>d</mi><mtext>out</mtext></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>14336</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d_{\text{out}}=14336</annotation></semantics></math> would consume nearly 1 GB per module call. We avoid this by performing sequence-level gating, where the same set of bases is selected for all tokens in a sequence. The gating indices have shape <math id="S3.SS1.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="[B,k]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mi>B</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>k</mi><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">[B,k]</annotation></semantics></math> rather than <math id="S3.SS1.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="[B,T,k]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mi>B</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>T</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">[B,T,k]</annotation></semantics></math>, and the gathered matrices have shape <math id="S3.SS1.p3.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="[B,k,d_{\text{out}},r]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mi>B</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>k</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>d</mi><mtext>out</mtext></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>r</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">[B,k,d_{\text{out}},r]</annotation></semantics></math>, reducing memory by a factor of <math id="S3.SS1.p3.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>T</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T</annotation></semantics></math>. The factored computation then proceeds as:</p>
<table id="S3.EGx1" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_align ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody id="S3.E3"><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S3.E3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle h" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>h</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle h</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S3.E3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle=\text{einsum}(\texttt{`bti,bkri-&gt;btkr'},x,B_{\mathcal{S}})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>=</mo><mrow><mtext>einsum</mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_monospace">‘bti,bkri-&gt;btkr’</mtext><mo>,</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>B</mi><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒮</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle=\text{einsum}(\texttt{`bti,bkri-&gt;btkr'},x,B_{\mathcal{S}})</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>

<tbody id="S3.E4"><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S3.E4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle\delta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>δ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle\delta</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S3.E4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle=\text{einsum}(\texttt{`btkr,bkor-&gt;btko'},h,A_{\mathcal{S}})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>=</mo><mrow><mtext>einsum</mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_monospace">‘btkr,bkor-&gt;btko’</mtext><mo>,</mo><mi>h</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>A</mi><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒮</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle=\text{einsum}(\texttt{`btkr,bkor-&gt;btko'},h,A_{\mathcal{S}})</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
