</figure>
<figure id="S5.F4" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2602.18628v1/fig1_loss_curve.svg" id="S5.F4.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:452/239;" width="452" height="239"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 4: </span>Training loss across sequential tasks. Task A trains on
Alpaca instruction-following data, converging to a loss of 0.77.
After region commitment, Task B trains on CodeAlpaca code generation
data with the lock loss active, converging to 0.95. The lock
constraint does not impede Task B learning.</figcaption>
</figure>
<figure id="S5.F5" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2602.18628v1/fig2_perplexity.svg" id="S5.F5.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:452/239;" width="452" height="239"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 5: </span>Training perplexity for both tasks. Task A achieves a
validation perplexity of 2.49 at convergence. Task B converges to a
perplexity of approximately 2.6, consistent with the increased
difficulty of code generation relative to general instruction following.</figcaption>
</figure>
<figure id="S5.F6" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2602.18628v1/fig12_comparison_table.svg" id="S5.F6.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/199;" width="476" height="199"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 6: </span>Comprehensive comparison of continual learning methods. NIWF
is the only method that achieves zero forgetting without requiring
external task labels at inference time. The 323M trainable parameter
count reflects conditional capacity, of which only half is active per
forward pass.</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S5.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Several observations emerge from Table <a href="#S5.T3" title="Table 3 ‣ 5.3 Results ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ Non-Interfering Weight Fields: Treating Model Parameters as a Continuously Extensible Function" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>. Full fine-tuning achieves the lowest perplexity on each task in isolation but suffers catastrophic forgetting of 85.5% on Task A after training on Task B. LoRA sequential training reduces forgetting compared to full fine-tuning but still degrades Task A by 39.9%. Maintaining separate LoRA adapters (one per task) preserves Task A perfectly but requires external routing and does not share capacity between tasks. NIWF achieves exact preservation of Task A (0% degradation) with competitive Task B performance, and does so through internal, learned routing with no external task labels at inference time.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS3.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS3.p3.1" class="ltx_p">The slightly higher perplexity of NIWF compared to task-specific LoRA (4.35 vs 4.21 on Task A, 4.62 vs 4.55 on Task B) reflects the overhead of the gating mechanism and the constraint that bases must support conditional selection. This is analogous to the small overhead of compiler optimizations for modularity. The guarantee of zero forgetting is worth the modest cost.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS4" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">5.4 </span>Ablation Studies</h3>

<figure id="S5.F7" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2602.18628v1/figC_ablation_bars.svg" id="S5.F7.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/218;" width="476" height="218"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 7: </span>Ablation and sensitivity analysis. Row (a), removing the
lock loss causes 30.6 percent forgetting, confirming it as critical.
Removing dynamics degrades both tasks. Row (b), perplexity improves
smoothly with rank and base count. Top-k sparsity trades a small
accuracy margin for constant-cost inference.</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S5.SS4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Figure <a href="#S5.F7" title="Figure 7 ‣ 5.4 Ablation Studies ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ Non-Interfering Weight Fields: Treating Model Parameters as a Continuously Extensible Function" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7</span></a> reveals the contribution of each component. Removing the coordinate dynamics and using a fixed random <math id="S5.SS4.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="z" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>z</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">z</annotation></semantics></math> increases perplexity on both tasks, confirming that input-dependent navigation provides meaningful adaptation. Removing the separation loss causes a small amount of forgetting (0.2%), indicating that without explicit encouragement to find new regions, Task B’s optimization occasionally drifts into Task A’s committed territory, causing minor lock loss violations. Removing the lock loss entirely results in 30.6% forgetting, demonstrating that without the functional constraint, the field freely modifies its behavior for Task A’s coordinates during Task B training. Using dense gating (all bases active, no top-<math id="S5.SS4.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> selection) slightly reduces Task A perplexity but increases Task B perplexity and removes the sparsity benefit that enables capacity scaling.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS5" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">5.5 </span>Coordinate Space Visualization</h3>

<figure id="S5.F8" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2602.18628v1/fig6_tsne_coordinates.svg" id="S5.F8.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:310/284;" width="310" height="284"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 8: </span>t-SNE projection of capability coordinates after two-task
training. Task A and Task B coordinates form well-separated clusters.
The committed region ellipse, derived from the Mahalanobis distance
at the 95th percentile, tightly encloses the Task A cluster. The
separation loss pushes Task B coordinates to a distinct region.</figcaption>
</figure>
<figure id="S5.F9" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2602.18628v1/figD_coordinate_heatmap.png" id="S5.F9.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/174;" width="476" height="174" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 9: </span>Coordinate space analysis. Left, hexbin density of Task A
coordinates with the committed region boundary. Center, scatter of
both task coordinates showing clean separation. Right, Mahalanobis
distance histograms confirming that Task B samples fall well outside
the committed region boundary at tau.</figcaption>
</figure>
<figure id="S5.F10" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2602.18628v1/figE_gating_boxplot.svg" id="S5.F10.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:262/238;" width="262" height="238"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 10: </span>Distribution of gating entropy across transformer layers.
Deeper layers exhibit more concentrated gating, indicating
increasing specialization of adapter base selection. Diamond
markers show layer means.</figcaption>
</figure>
<figure id="S5.F11" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2602.18628v1/figF_gating_heatmap.png" id="S5.F11.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/209;" width="476" height="209" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 11: </span>Per-layer gating weight heatmaps. Task A and Task B
activate distinct subsets of adapter bases across layers, confirming
that the weight field learns task-specific routing without explicit
supervision. Different colormaps emphasize the non-overlapping
activation patterns.</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S5.SS5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To understand how NIWF organizes capabilities in coordinate space, we collect the <math id="S5.SS5.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="z_{1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>z</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">z_{1}</annotation></semantics></math> coordinates produced by the dynamics module on 400 validation examples from each task after the full two-task training protocol. We project the 64-dimensional coordinates to 2D using t-SNE.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS5.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS5.p2.1" class="ltx_p">The visualization reveals clean separation between the two tasks’ coordinate clusters, with the committed region boundary (derived from the Mahalanobis distance threshold) enclosing Task A’s cluster tightly. Task B’s coordinates occupy a distinct region of the space, pushed away by the separation loss. This confirms that the coordinate dynamics module learns to navigate to different regions for different input types, and that the commitment protocol successfully partitions the space.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S6" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">6 </span>Analysis</h2>

<section id="S6.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">6.1 </span>Why Functional Locking is Stronger Than Parameter Regularization</h3>

<figure id="S6.F12" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2602.18628v1/figI_lock_convergence.svg" id="S6.F12.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/161;" width="476" height="161"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 12: </span>Left, cumulative forgetting on Task 1 as tasks accumulate.
EWC forgetting grows monotonically due to approximate Fisher
estimates. NIWF maintains zero forgetting through exact functional
locking. Right, lock loss convergence for different lambda values.
Higher lambda produces faster convergence to preservation.</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S6.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">EWC and related methods compute an importance matrix <math id="S6.SS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Omega" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi mathvariant="normal">Ω</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Omega</annotation></semantics></math> and add a penalty <math id="S6.SS1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sum_{i}\Omega_{i}(\theta_{i}-\theta_{i}^{*})^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mo>∑</mo><mi>i</mi></msub><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">Ω</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>θ</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>−</mo><msubsup><mi>θ</mi><mi>i</mi><mo>∗</mo></msubsup></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sum_{i}\Omega_{i}(\theta_{i}-\theta_{i}^{*})^{2}</annotation></semantics></math> that discourages changes to important parameters. This has several weaknesses. The importance estimate is approximate (typically the diagonal of the Fisher information, which ignores parameter interactions). The penalty is soft, so large gradients on new tasks can override it. As tasks accumulate, the penalties from different tasks conflict, creating an increasingly constrained optimization landscape.</p>
</div>
<div id="S6.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">NIWF’s lock loss (Equation <a href="#S3.E13" title="In 3.5 Region Commitment and Functional Locking ‣ 3 Method ‣ Non-Interfering Weight Fields: Treating Model Parameters as a Continuously Extensible Function" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">13</span></a>) avoids all of these issues. It operates on function outputs rather than parameters, so it captures the full input-output behavior of the field regardless of how parameters are organized internally. The constraint is enforced at specific anchor points with zero tolerance, not through a weighted penalty. Different committed regions do not conflict because they occupy distinct portions of the coordinate space. The field is free to change its parameters however it likes, as long as the outputs at anchor points are preserved.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S6.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">6.2 </span>Capacity Scaling Properties</h3>

<figure id="S6.F13" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2602.18628v1/fig9_capacity_scaling.svg" id="S6.F13.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/174;" width="476" height="174"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 13: </span>Left, stored versus active parameter scaling as the number
of bases increases. Active computation remains constant at k equals 8
bases regardless of total capacity. Right, coordinate space utilization
as tasks accumulate. The 64-dimensional space supports dozens of
committed regions before expansion is needed.</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S6.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">A natural question is how NIWF scales as the number of tasks grows. There are two dimensions of scaling to consider.</p>
</div>
<div id="S6.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Coordinate space capacity. The coordinate space <math id="S6.SS2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbb{R}^{d_{z}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>z</mi></msub></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbb{R}^{d_{z}}</annotation></semantics></math> is continuous and high-dimensional (<math id="S6.SS2.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="d_{z}=64" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>z</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>64</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d_{z}=64</annotation></semantics></math> in our experiments). With Gaussian regions and the 95th percentile threshold, each committed region occupies a bounded ellipsoid. The number of non-overlapping ellipsoids that can fit in a bounded region of <math id="S6.SS2.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbb{R}^{64}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mn>64</mn></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbb{R}^{64}</annotation></semantics></math> is astronomical, far exceeding any practical number of tasks.</p>
</div>
<div id="S6.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.SS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Adapter base capacity. The adapter banks have a fixed number of bases <math id="S6.SS2.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N_{b}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>N</mi><mi>b</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N_{b}</annotation></semantics></math>. Different tasks may share bases (when the weight field learns to activate the same bases for related tasks) or use disjoint subsets (for unrelated tasks). When the bases become saturated, the system can be expanded by increasing <math id="S6.SS2.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N_{b}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>N</mi><mi>b</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N_{b}</annotation></semantics></math> and adding freshly initialized bases. The lock loss ensures that committed regions are preserved during and after expansion, since the field’s outputs on committed anchors are constrained regardless of how many total bases exist.</p>
</div>
<div id="S6.SS2.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.SS2.p4.1" class="ltx_p">This gives NIWF an appealing scaling profile. The per-token computational cost is bounded by <math id="S6.SS2.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="O(k)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>O</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>k</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">O(k)</annotation></semantics></math> regardless of total capacity, and total capacity can be increased post-hoc without retraining existing capabilities.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S6.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">6.3 </span>Comparison with Mixture-of-Experts</h3>

<div id="S6.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">MoE architectures share NIWF’s principle of conditional computation but differ in several fundamental ways. MoE routes individual tokens to expert subnetworks based on a learned gating function, with no memory across tokens or sequences. NIWF routes entire sequences (via the coordinate dynamics) to regions of capability space, with smooth navigation enabled by the GRU dynamics. MoE experts are full sublayers with all parameters mutable during training. NIWF bases are low-rank deltas on a frozen backbone, with functional locking for committed regions. MoE has no concept of commitment, versioning, or rollback. NIWF provides all three as first-class operations.</p>
</div>
<div id="S6.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.SS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">These differences make NIWF suitable for deployment scenarios where MoE is not. Specifically, any scenario requiring sequential capability addition with guaranteed preservation of existing capabilities benefits from NIWF’s design.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S7" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">7 </span>Broader Vision: Software-Like Versioning for Intelligence</h2>

<div id="S7.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S7.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The NIWF framework introduces a fundamentally different way of thinking about model development. Rather than treating a trained model as a monolithic artifact that must be replaced wholesale, NIWF enables an incremental development model analogous to software engineering.</p>
</div>
<div id="S7.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S7.p2.1" class="ltx_p">In software engineering, a codebase is organized into modules. Each module has a well-defined interface. Changes to one module do not affect others as long as the interface is respected. Releases are versioned. Faulty updates can be rolled back. Multiple teams can develop features in parallel and merge them without conflict.</p>
</div>
<div id="S7.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S7.p3.1" class="ltx_p">NIWF provides analogous properties for neural network intelligence. Each committed region is a module with a well-defined functional interface (the field’s output on the region’s anchors). Changes outside the region do not affect the committed capability. The commitment protocol creates an immutable version of each capability. Removing a committed region from the lock loss effectively rolls back that capability. Two independently trained regions can coexist in the same coordinate space as long as they do not overlap, enabling parallel development.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S8" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">8 </span>Limitations</h2>

<div id="S8.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S8.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Certain limitations of the current work should be acknowledged. First, the two-pass forward strategy doubles inference latency compared to the base model. Amortization strategies (caching the first pass, training a fast <math id="S8.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="z" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>z</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">z</annotation></semantics></math> predictor) could reduce this overhead but are not extensively explored here. Second, our experiments are limited to two sequential tasks on a 7B model. Validating the framework at the scale of dozens of tasks on models with 70B or more parameters is necessary to confirm the scaling properties we describe analytically. Third, the region commitment protocol assumes that coordinate distributions are approximately Gaussian, which may not hold for tasks with multimodal distributions in coordinate space. Non-parametric density estimation could address this but would increase the complexity of the commitment step.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S9" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">9 </span>Conclusion</h2>

<div id="S9.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S9.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We have presented Non-Interfering Weight Fields, a framework that replaces the fixed weight paradigm in neural networks with a continuously extensible function over a capability coordinate space. By generating weight configurations on demand and functionally freezing committed coordinate regions, NIWF provides a structural guarantee against catastrophic forgetting that is fundamentally stronger than existing regularization-based or replay-based approaches. The framework introduces the notion of software-like versioning for neural network intelligence, where capabilities can be committed, extended, composed, and rolled back through operations on the coordinate space rather than on the weight vector itself.</p>
</div>
<div id="S9.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S9.p2.1" class="ltx_p">The experiments on Mistral-7B demonstrate the feasibility of the approach, with zero forgetting on committed tasks and competitive perplexity on new tasks, all within the memory constraints of a single 24 GB consumer GPU. While the current demonstration is small in scale, the architectural principles of NIWF, namely conditional computation via sparse gating, continuous coordinate spaces with learned dynamics, and functional locking via anchor-based constraints, are general and scale-independent.</p>
</div>
<div id="S9.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S9.p3.1" class="ltx_p">We believe that the transition from fixed weights to weight fields represents a conceptual shift of similar magnitude to the transitions from hand-crafted features to learned representations and from recurrent processing to attention. Models should not be pottery, fired once and forever fragile. They should be living systems that grow with every new capability, never losing what they have already learned.</p>
</div>
</section>

<div id="A1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">The per-module parameter count for the adapter bank is <math id="A1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N_{b}\cdot r\cdot(d_{\text{in}}+d_{\text{out}})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>N</mi><mi>b</mi></msub><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">⋅</mo><mi>r</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">⋅</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>d</mi><mtext>in</mtext></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>d</mi><mtext>out</mtext></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N_{b}\cdot r\cdot(d_{\text{in}}+d_{\text{out}})</annotation></semantics></math>. Summing over all modules, multiplying by 32 layers, and using <math id="A1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N_{b}=16" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>N</mi><mi>b</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>16</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N_{b}=16</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="A1.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r=8" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>8</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r=8</annotation></semantics></math>, the total adapter parameter count is:</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<table id="A1.E15" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A1.E15.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\begin{split}P&amp;=32\times 16\times 8\times(4096+4096+4096+1024+4096+1024\\
&amp;\quad+1024+4096+4096+14336+4096+14336+14336+4096)\\
&amp;\approx 323\text{M}\end{split}" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mtable columnspacing="0pt" displaystyle="true" rowspacing="0pt"><mtr><mtd class="ltx_align_right" columnalign="right"><mi>P</mi></mtd><mtd class="ltx_align_left" columnalign="left"><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>=</mo><mrow><mn>32</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mn>16</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mn>8</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mn>4096</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>4096</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>4096</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>1024</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>4096</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>1024</mn></mrow><mo fence="true" lspace="0em">CLOSE</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd></mtd><mtd class="ltx_align_left" columnalign="left"><mrow><mo fence="true" rspace="0em">OPEN</mo><mrow><mrow><mo>+</mo><mn>1024</mn></mrow><mo>+</mo><mn>4096</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>4096</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>14336</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>4096</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>14336</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>14336</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>4096</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd></mtd><mtd class="ltx_align_left" columnalign="left"><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>≈</mo><mrow><mn>323</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mtext>M</mtext></mrow></mrow></mtd></mtr></mtable><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\begin{split}P&amp;=32\times 16\times 8\times(4096+4096+4096+1024+4096+1024\\
&amp;\quad+1024+4096+4096+14336+4096+14336+14336+4096)\\
&amp;\approx 323\text{M}\end{split}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(15)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div>
<div id="A1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">At 4 bytes per parameter (float32), this requires approximately 1.29 GB. With AdamW optimizer states (momentum and variance), the total is approximately 3.88 GB.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A2" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix B </span>Commit Protocol Details</h2>

<div id="A2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The anchor sampling procedure samples points from the fitted Gaussian distribution and rejects those falling outside the Mahalanobis distance threshold. Specifically, we draw candidates <math id="A2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="z\sim\mathcal{N}(\mu,\Sigma)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>z</mi><mo>∼</mo><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒩</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>μ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Σ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">z\sim\mathcal{N}(\mu,\Sigma)</annotation></semantics></math>, compute <math id="A2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="d_{M}(z,\mu,\Sigma)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>M</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>z</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>μ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Σ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d_{M}(z,\mu,\Sigma)</annotation></semantics></math>, and accept those with <math id="A2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="d_{M}\leq\tau" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>M</mi></msub><mo>≤</mo><mi>τ</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d_{M}\leq\tau</annotation></semantics></math>. This process is repeated until 256 anchors are collected. In practice, with a 95th percentile threshold, approximately 95% of candidates are accepted, so the rejection sampling converges quickly.</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">The snapshot records the full output of the weight field on each anchor, which has shape <math id="A2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="[L\times N_{b}]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mi>L</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msub><mi>N</mi><mi>b</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">[L\times N_{b}]</annotation></semantics></math> per anchor. For 256 anchors with <math id="A2.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="L=32" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>L</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>32</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">L=32</annotation></semantics></math> layers and <math id="A2.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N_{b}=16" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>N</mi><mi>b</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>16</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N_{b}=16</annotation></semantics></math> bases, the snapshot requires <math id="A2.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="256\times 32\times 16\times 4=524" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mn>256</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mn>32</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mn>16</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>524</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">256\times 32\times 16\times 4=524</annotation></semantics></math> KB, which is negligible.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A3" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix C </span>Implementation Notes</h2>

<div id="A3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The NIWFLinear module replaces the standard <span id="A3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">forward</span> method of each target linear layer via monkey-patching. Before each backbone forward pass, the current gating decisions (top-<math id="A3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> indices and weights) are computed from the weight field and stored in a dictionary keyed by module name. Each monkey-patched forward method reads its gating decisions from this dictionary, computes the factored adapter output using the einsum operations in Equations <a href="#S3.E3" title="In 3.1 Frozen Backbone with Conditional Adapter Banks ‣ 3 Method ‣ Non-Interfering Weight Fields: Treating Model Parameters as a Continuously Extensible Function" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>–<a href="#S3.E4" title="In 3.1 Frozen Backbone with Conditional Adapter Banks ‣ 3 Method ‣ Non-Interfering Weight Fields: Treating Model Parameters as a Continuously Extensible Function" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>, and adds it to the base linear output.</p>
</div>
<div id="A3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">This approach avoids modifying any backbone code and is compatible with HuggingFace <span id="A3.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">transformers</span> models that use <span id="A3.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">device_map="auto"</span> for model parallelism.</p>
</div>
<div id="A3.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.p3.1" class="ltx_p">The adapter bank parameters (<math id="A3.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="A" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>A</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">A</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="A3.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="B" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>B</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">B</annotation></semantics></math> matrices) are stored in float32 even when the backbone uses bfloat16. This is because the low-rank bottleneck (<math id="A3.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r=8" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>8</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r=8</annotation></semantics></math>) makes the adapter computation sensitive to numerical precision, and the memory cost of float32 adapter parameters (1.29 GB) is modest compared to the total budget.</p>
</div>
</section>
</article>
</div>
